clue.text: Solitary poet, suffering in letters

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase, matching the adjective answer

indicators.note: something suffering is knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the twelve letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A lonely poet pours out his misery in correspondence.
explanation.definitionFit: Epistolatory is an old variant of epistolary, describing what is written or conducted by means of correspondence.

clue.text: Haughtiness a playwright is showing in London museum

indicators.note: the words before it are placed inside the museum named after it

parts.note: George Bernard Shaw, the Irish dramatist

explanation.surface: A dramatist puts on airs while appearing at a museum in London.
explanation.walkthrough: A bashaw is an old form of pasha, a Turkish governor, so the answer is the lordly arrogance of one.
explanation.definitionFit: Bashawism is the pompous, overbearing manner of a pasha, which is a form of arrogance.

clue.text: Article fine, no longer distorted

definitions.note: 'no longer' marks the answer as an obsolete word

parts.note: to sconce is to fine, an old Oxford university usage

explanation.surface: A piece of writing is cleared up so that it is no longer garbled.
explanation.walkthrough: Sconce as a verb meaning to fine is college slang, once used for penalising breaches of table etiquette.
explanation.definitionFit: Asconce is an obsolete form of askance, meaning awry or sideways, hence twisted out of true.

clue.text: Stalk as one nasty pest going about

indicators.note: going about means surrounding, so the rearranged word wraps the other piece
nasty suggests the word is mangled, so its letters are shuffled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A gardener spots an unpleasant bug crawling round a stem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As' is only a link here; the shuffled insect is split so the numeral can sit in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A stipe is the botanical term for the stalk of a mushroom, fern frond or seaweed.

clue.text: Silence of one studying the past briefly

indicators.note: briefly asks for a shortened form, so most of the word is cut away

explanation.surface: A historian keeps a short, stern silence.
explanation.walkthrough: HIST is the standard abbreviation for historian.
explanation.definitionFit: Hist is an old interjection used to command quiet, the equivalent of shush, so it stands for a call for silence.

clue.text: I and others hugging old lover may display old-style passion

indicators.note: something hugging another wraps around it, so the first word encloses the second

parts.note: the speaker plus others is we
an ex is a former partner

explanation.surface: A group of friends embrace a former flame and show their emotion in the old way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wax' can mean a fit of anger, as in 'in a wax', and the answer is Spenser's spelling of that word.
explanation.definitionFit: Wexe is an archaic spelling of wax, which in the sense of a temper or rage is a passion.

clue.text: Trendy soul cheers, embracing husband in African movement

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so the last piece wraps the letter that follows it

parts.note: in Egyptian belief the ka is the spiritual double or soul

explanation.surface: A cool spirit applauds as a married man joins an African campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: Ta is British informal thanks, and the ka is the Egyptian idea of a person's spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: Inkatha is the Zulu cultural and political movement in South Africa, later the Inkatha Freedom Party.

clue.text: English patron saint getting rid of smoking brute finally gets affection

indicators.note: getting rid of means taking letters out of the saint's name

parts.note: St George is England's patron saint

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of each of the two words before it

parts.note: the final letters of the two words

explanation.surface: St George loses a fire-breathing monster and is rewarded with love.
explanation.walkthrough: The first G and E in ST GEORGE are removed, leaving ST+ORGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Storge is the Greek word for natural familial affection, especially of parents for children.

clue.text: In India, European is very much at home — gosh!

parts.note: far as in far better, by a lot
being in means being at home

explanation.surface: A European in India feels thoroughly at home, much to his surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Faringee is an Anglo-Indian form of feringhee, the term in India for a European or foreigner.

clue.text: Greek princess who could be calm yet stern

indicators.note: could be suggests the following letters might form something else once reordered

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A description of a royal Greek woman's composed but severe temperament.
explanation.walkthrough: Fitting surface: Clytemnestra coolly plotted the murder of her husband Agamemnon.
explanation.definitionFit: Clytemnestra, daughter of the Spartan king Tyndareus, was a princess of Greek legend and later queen of Mycenae.

clue.text: Detestable patient is 'ell to deal with

indicators.note: dealing with something means working it over, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, with 'ell' as the letters ELL

explanation.surface: A doctor complains that a horrid patient is hell to manage.
explanation.definitionFit: Pestilential, literally plague-bearing, is used figuratively of anything hateful or annoying.

clue.text: Cut in old-fashioned allowance reported

indicators.note: reported means passed on by word of mouth, so we want a word with the same sound

parts.note: size was once a fixed allowance of food or drink, as in a Cambridge sizar's ration

explanation.surface: Someone's antique stipend has been reduced, so the reports say.
explanation.definitionFit: To incise is to cut into a surface, as an engraver or surgeon does.

clue.text: Boat may be so ancient with its prow missing

indicators.note: the prow is the front of a boat, so the first letter goes

explanation.surface: An old vessel has lost its bow.
explanation.definitionFit: Oary means having or using oars, so a rowing boat could be described that way.

clue.text: Slap down local prisoners returning

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the word is read from end to start

explanation.surface: Local inmates coming back to jail get a smack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slap down' looks like one phrase; the definition is 'Slap', with 'down local' saying the sense is regional.
explanation.definitionFit: Swop, like swap, is a dialect word for a blow or to strike, the same as a slap.

clue.text: Place for animals — a couple used their teeth, said Spooner (7, two words)

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts are exchanged

explanation.surface: Spooner reports that two people bit into something somewhere animals are kept.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of 'pair bit' and you get the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bear pit is a sunken enclosure where bears were kept or baited, so a place for animals.

clue.text: Silver in starry decorative feature

indicators.note: the first item goes inside the word that follows

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A silver ornament set into a star-spangled design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silver in starry' reads like a hidden word, but no answer lurks there; the chemical symbol goes inside a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: An astragal is a small convex moulding round a column, an architectural ornament.

clue.text: Scratch from pussy left embedded

indicators.note: embedded means set inside, so one piece goes within the other

explanation.surface: A cat's claw mark is left stuck in someone's skin.
explanation.walkthrough: L goes into CAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Clat is a Scots and northern dialect word meaning to scratch or scrape.

clue.text: Old-style lesson in Latin before

parts.note: ere is a poetic word for before

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned schoolroom lesson in Latin before the others.
explanation.definitionFit: Lere is an archaic form of lore, meaning learning or a lesson.

clue.text: Priest and bishop in Lincoln

indicators.note: the first item is put inside the name that follows

explanation.surface: Clergy are gathered in the cathedral city of Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lincoln' looks like the English cathedral city, but it is Abraham Lincoln. B goes into ABE.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbé is a French title for an abbot or any clergyman.

clue.text: We hear advantage disappeared north of the border

indicators.note: we hear means it is what reaches the ear, so the spelling is ignored

parts.note: a gain is an advantage or benefit

explanation.surface: Rumour has it that a lead in Scotland has vanished.
explanation.definitionFit: Gane is the Scots past participle of go, i.e. gone; north of the border means in Scotland.

clue.text: Sort of mug using old recycled clues

indicators.note: recycled means processed and reshaped, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A crossword setter's cup made from reused old clues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mug' looks like a cup; here it is slang for a face or mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: An oscule is a small mouth or opening, as in a sponge, and mug is slang for the mouth or face.

clue.text: Famous person tackling a politician is able to provide some illumination

definitions.note: a descriptive definition for a noun

indicators.note: tackling suggests grabbing hold of, so the first word surrounds the others

parts.note: a lion is a celebrity, a social lion

explanation.surface: A celebrity grilling an MP can shed some light on things.
explanation.walkthrough: A MP goes inside LI...ON.
explanation.definitionFit: A lampion is an oil lamp, often coloured, used in illuminations, so it gives light.

clue.text: European beset by ruefulness may offer welcome again

indicators.note: beset by means surrounded by, so the first piece is placed within the second

explanation.surface: A sorry-looking European may still give a second greeting.
explanation.walkthrough: E goes into REGR...ET.
explanation.definitionFit: To regreet is to greet a second time, an archaic Shakespearean verb.

clue.text: This writer's housed in filthy places endlessly — an impossible situation?

indicators.note: housed in means lodged within another word
endlessly means the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: this writer is I, so this writer's is I'm

explanation.surface: A writer living in squalor wonders if things are hopeless.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the final letter of the pigsties is dropped before the contraction goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Stimie is a variant of stymie, a golf position where a ball blocks the putt, hence an impasse.

clue.text: Body parts that whale has enable swimming

indicators.note: swimming suggests the letters are moving about freely and settle in another order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A whale's anatomy is what makes it able to swim.
explanation.definitionFit: Baleen is the horny filtering plates in a whale's mouth, also called whalebone.

clue.text: Skill with inner energy brings reward as before

indicators.note: with inner says the following item sits inside the first one

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Talent with inner drive pays off, as people used to say.
explanation.walkthrough: E goes into AR...T. 'As before' marks an archaic word.
explanation.definitionFit: Aret is a Spenserian verb meaning to entrust or to award, hence an old word for reward.

clue.text: The first person meeting the Queen is a Muslim ruler

explanation.surface: An audience with the Queen turns out to involve an Islamic leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Meer is a variant of emir or amir, a title for a Muslim prince or commander.

clue.text: Dish with some herbal titbits

indicators.note: some means only a portion of the words that follow is taken

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word and start of the next

explanation.surface: A meal served with herb nibbles on the side.
explanation.definitionFit: A balti is a spicy curry cooked and served in a wok-like pan, a dish popular in Birmingham.

clue.text: Bad foot? Bandages may be put round one left twisted

indicators.note: twisted means turned round, so the pair of letters is read backwards
put round means wrapped about the other piece

explanation.surface: An injured foot is strapped up after being turned on the left side.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'Bad foot' is a loose description of a medical condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Talipes is the medical term for club foot, a deformed foot, hence a bad one.

clue.text: State has set up gallery on many sites

indicators.note: in a down entry set up means raised, so the word reads bottom to top

parts.note: the Tate has galleries in London, Liverpool and St Ives

explanation.surface: The government has opened an art gallery across several locations.
explanation.definitionFit: Etat is French for state, used in English in coup d'état and état-major.

clue.text: Unanswerable question in holy book putting rector off

indicators.note: putting off a rector means taking out the abbreviation for one

explanation.surface: A puzzling query in a scripture that discourages the vicar.
explanation.walkthrough: R, the abbreviation for rector, comes out of KORAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A koan is a Zen Buddhist riddle with no logical answer, set to aid meditation.

clue.text: God has half the angels returning

indicators.note: returning means coming back, so the kept letters are read right to left
half means only the first half of the word is kept

parts.note: seraphim are the highest order of angels

explanation.surface: A deity has half his heavenly host coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: SERAPHIM halves to SERA, which reversed gives ARES.
explanation.definitionFit: Ares is the Greek god of war, counterpart of the Roman Mars.

clue.text: Old school characters in a group

parts.note: a gam is a school of whales

explanation.surface: A former school's lettering is grouped together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old school' reads as one phrase, but it is two pieces. Gam is a school of whales, not a place of learning.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogam, or ogham, is the ancient Irish alphabet whose strokes are arranged in groups, so its letters are characters in a group.

clue.text: Observe fast, full of melancholy, as of old

definitions.text: full of melancholy, as of old

parts.note: to do or keep a custom is to observe it

explanation.surface: Keeping a fast made people glum in the old days.
explanation.definitionFit: Dolent is an archaic adjective meaning sorrowful or mournful, close to melancholy.

clue.text: See ham moon in a true drama dreadfully rendered (12, two words)

indicators.note: the moon goes inside the rearranged phrase
something rendered dreadfully is performed badly, so the letters come out in a mangled order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
Io is one of Jupiter's moons

explanation.surface: A hammy actor overplays a moon scene in a realistic play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ham' suggests a bad actor, which the drama surface encourages; it is a radio enthusiast.
explanation.definitionFit: A ham is the informal name for a licensed amateur radio operator.

clue.text: Valuable material, as before, penned by yesteryear's left-winger?

indicators.note: penned by means enclosed within, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: a Bennite was a follower of Tony Benn on Labour's left in the 1980s
to means before, as in ten to six

explanation.surface: Precious goods are kept, as they used to be, by an old socialist.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Benn was a prominent left-wing British Labour politician; the question mark admits the coined-sounding follower word.
explanation.definitionFit: Bentonite is an absorbent clay with many industrial uses, so a useful material.
